pos: n. (the Overijssel town of the Brethren's house on the Agnietenberg, where Thomas a Kempis spent seventy years)
etymology: Dutch Zwolle, from Middle Dutch swol, a rise or hill, for the low ridge the town stands on between the Ijssel and the Vecht.
biblical_def: Zwolle is the Ijssel town whose school and whose cloister formed the inward religion of the northern Netherlands on the eve of the Reformation. Johannes Cele, rector of its town school from 1374 for forty years, built there one of the first graded schools in Europe, teaching in classes by age and ability and requiring Scripture of every boy, and his method was copied along the whole river. Just outside the walls, on the Agnietenberg, stood the Augustinian house of the Windesheim congregation where Thomas a Kempis lived from about 1399 until his death in 1471, copying the Bible four times over and writing the devotional pieces gathered as the Imitation of Christ. Zwolle thus produced both the schoolroom discipline and the book that shaped late medieval piety more than any other. The town went Reformed in the course of the revolt, produced the preacher Herman Moded, and its churches were ordered on the Dutch synodical pattern. The dictionary enters Zwolle because a graded school and a scriptorium are unglamorous things, and between them they put a Latin education and a legible Bible within reach of ordinary boys two generations before Luther.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cloister as a monastery or nunnery; a rector as the master of a school; transcription as the act of copying; and meditation as close or continued thought.
webster_full: CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a habitation for monks or nuns; an arcade or covered walk.
RECTOR, n. The master of a school; the chief elective officer of some universities; a clergyman who has the charge of a parish.
TRANSCRIPTION, n. The act of copying; transcript; a copy taken from an original.
MEDITATION, n. Close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind; serious contemplation.
SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.

Eph 6:4

Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: Overijssel town of Cele's graded school and the Agnietenberg cloister, where Thomas a Kempis copied the Bible and wrote the Imitation of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is a devotion turned wholly inward, which is the standing fault of the Imitation and of the house that produced it. The book teaches self-knowledge, contempt of the world and the quieting of the will, and it says little about the imputed righteousness by which a troubled conscience is actually settled. The dictionary reads it as a true account of the soul's disorder and an incomplete account of its cure, and notes that the piety it taught was not able to reform the mass that stood at the centre of the cloister's own day.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is meditation on the written word rather than on the self, which is what Scripture actually enjoins. “his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2) gives meditation an object outside the man, as does the charge to Joshua that “thou shalt meditate therein day and night” (Jos 1:8). Zwolle's school obeyed the other half of the pattern well, the teaching of children at close quarters, which the law lays on fathers: “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7).

pos: n. (the Ijssel town whose Brethren's school was the best in northern Europe, and whose press was among the earliest in the Netherlands)
etymology: Dutch Deventer, from a personal name or a Frankish settlement term; the town was a Hanseatic staple on the Ijssel.
biblical_def: Deventer is the town whose school taught the northern Renaissance and, by consequence, much of the Reformation. Its Latin school, run in close connection with the Brethren of the Common Life, reached eight or nine hundred boys under the rectorship of Alexander Hegius from 1483, and its curriculum put good Latin, some Greek and constant Scripture in front of sons of merchants and farmers; Erasmus was a pupil there, and so were a generation of men who later taught in the German and Dutch universities. The town also had one of the earliest presses in the Low Countries, printing from 1477, and for decades it produced schoolbooks and devotional works in quantity. In the revolt Deventer changed hands repeatedly, was betrayed to Spain by its English governor Sir William Stanley in 1587, and was retaken by Maurice in 1591, after which it was firmly Reformed; Caspar Sibelius was its minister and chronicler in the next century. The dictionary enters Deventer because the Reformation needed men who could read Greek and Hebrew and argue a text, and the schools that made such men were in place before there was a Reformation to use them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a grammar school as a school for teaching the languages; a staple as a settled market; to betray as to deliver into enemy hands treacherously; and erudition as learning acquired by study.
webster_full: GRAMMAR SCHOOL, n. A school in which the learned languages are taught, as Latin and Greek.
STAPLE, n. A settled mart or market; the principal commodity of a place; an established town of trade.
BETRAY, v. To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust.
ERUDITION, n. Learning; knowledge gained by study, or from books and instruction, particularly of the languages.
RECTOR, n. The master of a school; the head of a college or academy.

corruption_summary: Ijssel town whose Latin school under Hegius taught Erasmus and the northern humanists, and whose press printed from 1477.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the contempt for learning that dresses itself as piety, and Deventer is the standing argument against it. The men who translated the Scriptures into every tongue of Europe, collated manuscripts, and answered Rome text by text had to be taught Greek and Hebrew first, by schoolmasters who were not themselves famous. The duty is laid on every man who would answer an objector: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15), and readiness of that kind is not spontaneous.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the early and thorough teaching of children, on the promise that “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). Deventer also produced a cautionary case the dictionary records: Erasmus, its most famous pupil, had the learning and declined the Reformation, which shows that scholarship is an instrument and not a conversion. The habit worth keeping is the Berean one, of men who “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11), and a workman so trained “needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15).

pos: n. (the Zeeland port, Dutch Vlissingen, which drove out its Spanish garrison in April 1572 and held the mouth of the Scheldt)
etymology: English Flushing, an anglicising of Dutch Vlissingen, probably from a personal name or from vlis, a channel; it stands on Walcheren at the Scheldt's mouth.
biblical_def: Flushing is the town whose townsmen, not an army, began the Dutch revolt in earnest. On 1 April 1572 the Sea Beggars took Brielle; on 6 April the people of Flushing refused to admit a Spanish garrison, expelled the king's officers, killed the engineer sent to build a citadel over them, and declared for the Prince of Orange. Because Flushing stands on Walcheren at the mouth of the Scheldt, its revolt closed the sea road to Antwerp and opened it to the rebels, and the whole subsequent shape of the war followed from that: Zeeland and Holland could be supplied and reinforced by water, and the Spanish army could not be. The town was handed to Elizabeth of England in 1585 as one of the cautionary towns pledged against her loan and garrisoned by English troops under Sir Philip Sidney until 1616. Its church was strictly Reformed and its seamen carried the psalm book as well as the cutlass. The dictionary enters Flushing because the revolt that produced the Dutch Reformed republic was begun by shipmen and townsmen acting on their own, and the dictionary neither hides that nor pretends their motives were purely religious.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a garrison as troops stationed in a fort; a citadel as a fortress commanding a city; a cautionary town as one held in pledge; and an estuary as an arm of the sea.
webster_full: GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town to defend it against an enemy.
CITADEL, n. A fortress or castle in or near a city, intended for its defense, or to command and keep the inhabitants in subjection.
PLEDGE, n. Something deposited as security for the performance of a contract; a surety; a hostage.
ESTUARY, n. An arm of the sea; a frith; a narrow passage or the mouth of a river where the tide meets the current.
TOWNSMAN, n. An inhabitant of a town; one of the same town with another.

corruption_summary: Zeeland port on Walcheren which expelled its Spanish garrison on 6 April 1572, closing the Scheldt to Spain and opening the sea to the revolt.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the telling of a revolt as pure religion when taxes and garrisons were also in it. Flushing's townsmen objected to the tenth penny, to billeting and to a citadel built to overawe them, as well as to the Inquisition, and the dictionary says so rather than manufacturing a cleaner story. It also holds that the religious cause was real and primary for many of them, and that the honest way to record a mixed motive is to name both parts. “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) applies to a rebel citadel as much as to a royal one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is lawful defence of households and congregations without pretending the defence is itself the gospel. Nehemiah's word to armed builders is the nearest thing in Scripture to what Flushing did: “fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses” (Neh 4:14). The seamen of Zeeland who did the fighting were also the men who carried the psalms into the ports of three continents, for they are among those “that go down to the sea in ships” (Psa 107:23) and the charge to “Declare his glory among the heathen” (Psa 96:3) went with them.

pos: n. (the Scheldt port that was the richest city of northern Europe, the Reformation's printing house, and whose fall in 1585 built Amsterdam)
etymology: Dutch Antwerpen, from aan de werpen, at the wharves, or from anda and werpum, a thrown-up bank; Latin Antverpia.
biblical_def: Antwerp was for sixty years the commercial capital of northern Europe and, because of that, the Reformation's chief printing city and most religiously mixed population. Luther's books were on sale there by 1518, and the Augustinian house whose prior was imprisoned and whose friars Voes and Van Esch were burned at Brussels in 1523 was Antwerp's. Tyndale's English New Testaments were printed and shipped from its quays. Christopher Plantin's press, the greatest in Europe, produced the Antwerp Polyglot between 1568 and 1573, the Scriptures in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Aramaic and Syriac in eight volumes under Spanish royal patronage, an instrument of textual study that served Protestant scholars for two centuries. The city held Lutheran, Reformed, Anabaptist and Catholic congregations at once; it suffered the Spanish Fury of 1576, tried a formal Religious Peace in 1578, and fell to Parma after a fourteen-month siege in August 1585. The terms gave Protestants four years to settle their affairs and leave, and some tens of thousands did, taking their trades, their capital and their ministers to Amsterdam, Leiden and Middelburg. The dictionary enters Antwerp because its ruin is the direct cause of the Dutch golden age, and because its press served the church that its king was trying to destroy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a polyglot as a book containing several languages; a quay as a mole or wharf; emigration as removal from one country to another; and a siege as the investing of a fortified place.
webster_full: POLYGLOT, a. Having or containing many languages; as a polyglot Bible or lexicon.
QUAY, n. A mole, bank or wharf formed toward the sea, or on the side of a river, for the loading of ships.
EMIGRATION, n. Removal of inhabitants from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
FURY, n. A violent rushing; impetuous motion; rage; a storm of anger or violence.

corruption_summary: Scheldt port, richest city of northern Europe and the Reformation's printing house, which fell to Parma in 1585 and sent its Protestants north.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the judgement that a catastrophe is simply a defeat. Antwerp fell, the Reformed church there was ended, and the greatest Protestant commercial centre in Europe was lost to the cause; by that reckoning 1585 was the Reformation's worst year in the Low Countries. What the emigration actually produced was the Dutch republic's capital, its universities' endowment and its printing trade, and the ministers who built the churches of Holland and Zeeland. “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (Gen 50:20) is the pattern, and Parma's terms of 1585 are a plain instance of it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is providence over the church's disasters, which is not a consolation offered instead of grief but a fact alongside it. “all things work together for good to them that love God” (Rom 8:28) does not make the siege less cruel or the exile less costly. The dictionary also notes how the dispersion worked, exactly as in Acts: “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4), and those who left Antwerp “travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch” (Act 11:19) in their own measure, which for them meant Amsterdam, London, Frankfurt and Hamburg.

pos: n. (the great Flemish town whose Calvinist republic of 1577 suppressed the mass by force and lost the south for the Reformation)
etymology: Dutch Gent, French Gand, from the Celtic condate, a confluence, for the meeting of the Lys and the Scheldt.
biblical_def: Ghent was the largest town of Flanders and the most turbulent, with a long tradition of guild risings against its counts, and in the revolt against Spain it put a Calvinist government in power and used it hard. The Pacification of Ghent in November 1576 had united the provinces, Catholic and Protestant together, against the Spanish soldiery on the understanding that each province would keep its own religion. Ghent broke that understanding. From 1577 Jan van Hembyze and Francois van Ryhove governed the town as a Calvinist republic, suppressed the mass, imprisoned the bishop, seized church property, forced the surrounding Flemish towns into the same settlement, and treated the Catholic nobility of the revolt as enemies. The southern provinces answered with the Union of Arras in January 1579; William of Orange came in person to Ghent to restrain Hembyze and failed; and Parma took the town in 1584. The dictionary enters Ghent as a judgement against our own side. Flanders was lost to the Reformation, and the loss was not only Spain's work: the Reformed party in Ghent had the mass abolished by magistrates and soldiers rather than preached down, and the provinces that might have gone with them went to the king instead.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a guild as a society or corporation; pacification as the act of making peace; to suppress as to crush or put an end to; and sedition as a commotion in a state.
webster_full: GUILD, n. A society, fraternity or corporation, associated for some common purpose, as of trade.
PACIFICATION, n. The act of making peace between parties at variance; the act of appeasing wrath.
SUPPRESS, v. To crush; to subdue; to put an end to; to overpower and destroy.
SEDITION, n. A factious commotion of the people; a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law or the administration.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, zeal is an eagerness of desire to accomplish an object.

corruption_summary: Great Flemish town whose Calvinist republic of 1577 suppressed the mass by force, provoked the Union of Arras, and fell to Parma in 1584.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is our own, and Ghent is where it is clearest. Hembyze's government had zeal, and the apostle's description of a zeal that misses its mark fits it exactly: “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). The mass is a corruption of the Lord's Supper and the dictionary says so without qualification; it was not Ghent's magistrates' business to end it by imprisoning a bishop and coercing neighbouring towns, and the direct consequence was that the Catholic nobility of the revolt signed with Spain and ten provinces were lost.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the means by which the church is actually built, which is not the magistrate's arm. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) was spoken over a building project, and “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4) is the apostolic rule for the same work. The temper is judged too, for “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jam 1:20), and the wrath in Ghent was on the Reformed side as well as the Spanish.

pos: n. (the decayed Flemish port whose foreign merchant colonies brought in the first Reformation books, and which remained Catholic)
etymology: Dutch Brugge, from the Old Norse bryggja or Germanic brugga, a landing stage or bridge; French Bruges.
biblical_def: Bruges is the Flemish town where the Reformation came in by the quayside and never took the town. In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries it had been the chief market of northern Europe, with permanent colonies of English, Spanish, Italian and Hanseatic merchants and their own houses and chapels; by the 1520s its channel to the sea had silted, Antwerp had taken its trade, and it was a declining city of some decayed grandeur. The foreign merchants were the opening: German and English traders brought in Lutheran books and Tyndale's New Testaments among their bales, and small conventicles met in the 1520s and 1530s. The authorities answered with the placards, and the Bruges accounts record executions for heresy through the middle of the century. No Reformed congregation of weight was ever gathered there. When Flanders divided, Bruges stayed with the king and with Rome, and it has been a Catholic town ever since. The dictionary enters Bruges as the ordinary case beside the famous ones. For every Antwerp or Ghent there were towns where the books arrived, a few men read them, some were burned, and the town went on as before, and the honest history of the Reformation includes them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conventicle as a private assembly for worship; a bale as a pack of goods; to silt as to fill with mud; and a colony as a body of people settled in a distant country.
webster_full: CONVENTICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; a secret or private assembly for religious worship, applied reproachfully.
BALE, n. A bundle or package of goods in a cloth cover, and corded for transportation.
SILT, n. Fine earth or mud deposited from running water; to fill or choke with such deposit.
COLONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.
DECAY, n. Gradual failure of health, strength, soundness, prosperity, or of any species of excellence.

corruption_summary: Decayed Flemish port whose foreign merchant colonies imported the first Reformation books, where men were executed for heresy and no Reformed church took root.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the history that only records successes, which flatters the cause and teaches nobody anything. Bruges had the books, the conventicles and the martyrs, and it has no Reformed congregation in its story; the seed fell and did not come up. The parable is plain that this is to be expected: “some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up” (Mat 13:4), and the Lord's own explanation names the agent, that the wicked one “catcheth away that which was sown in his heart” (Mat 13:19).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the labourers are not the ones who give the increase, and are therefore not the ones who are judged by it. “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) covers the merchant who carried a New Testament into Bruges in a bale of cloth and saw no church come of it. The promise is not that every sowing produces a visible harvest in the sower's town, but that the word accomplishes what it was sent for: “it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).

“but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) — Tyndale's New Testaments carried in among the bales.

pos: n. (the French-speaking town over whose castle wall the Belgic Confession was thrown to the king's officers in 1561)
etymology: French Tournai, Dutch Doornik, from the Celtic turno, a height, with a Latin suffix; the town stands on the Scheldt.
biblical_def: Tournai is the town where a confession of faith was delivered by being thrown over a wall. A French-speaking bishopric on the Scheldt, surrounded by Flemish-speaking country and long disputed between France and the Low Countries, it held from the 1540s one of the most determined Reformed congregations in the Netherlands, served at intervals by Guido de Bres. In September 1561 the congregation marched through the streets at night singing psalms, the demonstrations the authorities called the chanteries, and when the government demanded to know what these people believed, a copy of the newly written Confession of Faith of the Reformed Churches of the Low Countries was thrown over the wall of the castle with a letter addressed to Philip II: a statement that they held the magistrate's authority to be of God and would obey in all things civil, that they numbered many thousands, and that they would not give up the preaching of the word. Repression followed; de Bres fled and was taken six years later. Parma besieged and took the town in 1581, its defence conducted by Christine de Lalaing after her husband left. The dictionary enters Tournai because a confession written for a hostile king and delivered over a wall is the clearest picture of what confessing means.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary of articles of faith; to confess as to own or acknowledge; a bishopric as the diocese of a bishop; and a demonstration as a public exhibition or show.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a public acknowledgment of belief.
CONFESS, v. To own, acknowledge or avow, as a crime, a fault, a charge, a debt or a truth.
BISHOPRIC, n. A diocese; the district over which the jurisdiction of a bishop extends.
DEMONSTRATION, n. The act of demonstrating; a public exhibition or show of feeling or opinion.
WALL, n. A work or structure of stone, brick or other materials, raised to some height, and intended for defense or security.
scriptures: Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.
corruption_summary: French-speaking town on the Scheldt whose Reformed congregation delivered the Belgic Confession over the castle wall to Philip II's officers in 1561.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the private faith that will not be stated where it costs something, which the Tournai congregation refused by the manner of its delivery. They did not publish anonymously or petition for tolerance of an unnamed opinion; they wrote out what they believed, article by article, signed it as a body, and handed it to the officers of the king who was executing men for holding it. “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32) is the warrant, and a confession is the instrument by which a church does it corporately.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the public and verbal nature of faith, which Scripture makes part of salvation's own order: “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom 10:10). Timothy is reminded that he “hast professed a good profession before many witnesses” (1Ti 6:12), and the psalmist's resolve is the exact shape of what happened at Tournai: “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46).

“I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46) — a letter addressed to Philip II.
“hast professed a good profession before many witnesses” (1Ti 6:12) — the psalm-singing processions of the chanteries.

pos: n. (the Hainaut town that held out for the Reformed in 1566, was stormed in 1567, and where Guido de Bres was hanged)
etymology: French Valenciennes, from a Gallo-Roman estate name, perhaps of the emperor Valentinian; the town stands on the Scheldt in Hainaut.
biblical_def: Valenciennes is the town that made the first armed stand of the Dutch Reformation and lost it. Its Reformed congregation was among the oldest and boldest in the Walloon provinces; in 1562 the townspeople rescued two ministers from the stake and the psalm-singing processions that followed, the chanteries, were treated by the government as open rebellion. After the image-breaking of August 1566 the Reformed took effective control of the town, held public worship, and when the regent demanded a royal garrison in December they refused to admit it. Valenciennes was besieged through the winter, bombarded, and stormed on 23 March 1567, after which the executions began. Guido de Bres, who had come into the town to serve and strengthen the congregation during the siege, was captured in flight, imprisoned at Tournai and Valenciennes, examined at length, and hanged in the marketplace on 31 May 1567 with his fellow minister Peregrin de la Grange. His prison letters to his wife, his mother and his congregation were printed and circulated widely. The dictionary enters Valenciennes because the author of the Belgic Confession died there, and because a town that refused a garrison in December was storming distance from a Spanish army in March.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bombardment as an attack with shells; to storm as to assault and take by force; a marketplace as the place of public sale; and an epistle as a letter written and sent.
webster_full: BOMBARDMENT, n. An attack with bombs; the act of throwing bombs into a town, fort or ship.
STORM, v. To attack; to assault; to attempt to take by open force, as a fort or fortified town.
MARKETPLACE, n. The place where provisions or goods are exposed for sale; a public place in a town.
EPISTLE, n. A writing, directed or sent to a person or persons; a letter; a letter missive.
SCAFFOLD, n. A temporary gallery or stage raised either for shows or for the execution of a criminal.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
Phi 1:21
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: Hainaut town whose Reformed congregation refused a royal garrison in 1566, was stormed in March 1567, and where Guido de Bres was hanged on 31 May 1567.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the confusing of a congregation's cause with a town's defences. Valenciennes had the better doctrine and the worse walls, and the dictionary does not pretend the refusal of the garrison was a wise act; it was a brave one made by men who had already seen their ministers taken to the stake, and it ended in a storm, a sack and a scaffold. What is not in doubt is the manner of the dying. De Bres went into a besieged town to serve a congregation he could have left, and his own words from the prison are of a piece with the apostle's: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phi 1:21).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pastor's obligation to the flock in the hour when leaving would be reasonable. “neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy” (Act 20:24) is the charge de Bres accepted, and of his ending the plainest word is “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7). To the congregation he wrote to from the prison, the promise given to Smyrna applies: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).

pos: n. (the Brabant barony of the house of Orange-Nassau, twice besieged, and the Reformed garrison town of the Dutch frontier)
etymology: Dutch Breda, from brede Aa, the broad Aa, for the widening of the river at the town; the barony passed to the Nassaus in 1403.
biblical_def: Breda was the Brabant town that belonged personally to the house of Orange-Nassau, and it therefore stood where the Dutch Reformation and the Dutch war touched each other most directly. William of Orange held the barony, and the Reformation was established in the town under Nassau patronage; because it lay in Brabant, on the open southern side of the republic, it was also one of the most fought-over places in Europe. Spinola took it for Spain in June 1625 after a siege of eleven months in which both the garrison and the townspeople starved, a siege famous enough that Velazquez painted its surrender; Frederick Henry of Orange retook it in October 1637 after a siege of his own; and the Peace of Munster in 1648 left it Dutch. Its Great Church held the Nassau tombs. The dictionary enters Breda because it is the plainest instance in the Low Countries of a congregation whose standing rested on a prince's title to the ground it stood on, and because the ordinary members of that congregation paid for the prince's wars by eating their horses twice in twelve years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a barony as the lordship of a baron; a siege as the investing of a place; famine as scarcity of food; and a sepulchre as a place of burial.
webster_full: BARONY, n. The lordship, honor or fee of a baron, whether spiritual or temporal.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient to feed a people.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; a place where the dead body of a human being is interred.
PATRONAGE, n. Special countenance or support; favor or protection bestowed on a person or cause.
scriptures: Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
Hab 3:17

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
Rom 8:35
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
Psa 46:7
The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah.
corruption_summary: Brabant barony of the house of Orange-Nassau, Reformed under Nassau patronage, taken by Spinola in 1625 and retaken by Frederick Henry in 1637.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the confidence of a church in its prince, which Breda held and twice found insufficient. The barony was the Nassaus' own, the garrison was the republic's best, and in 1625 the town starved for eleven months and surrendered anyway. The psalm names the alternative exactly: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). Breda's people ate the horses, which is a blunt way of learning the distinction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is a faith that does not depend on the outcome of the siege. The prophet's resolve is the proper temper of a garrison town: “Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines” (Hab 3:17), he will yet rejoice in the Lord. And the apostle's list of what cannot separate the believer from Christ includes the two things Breda knew best, since he asks whether “tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine” (Rom 8:35) can do it. The town's true defence is the one the psalm names, that “The LORD of hosts is with us” (Psa 46:7).

pos: n. (the oldest town of the Netherlands, chief place of Gelderland, whose academy became a seat of the Cartesian controversy)
etymology: Dutch Nijmegen, from Latin Noviomagus, the new field or market; the Roman settlement is the oldest in the Netherlands.
biblical_def: Nijmegen is the Gelderland town where a Reformed academy made itself the forward position of the Cartesian quarrel. A Roman foundation and a favourite seat of Charlemagne, it was an imperial free city before it fell to the dukes of Gelderland, joined the revolt, was lost again, and was finally taken for the republic by Maurice of Nassau in 1591. In 1655 the town opened an Illustrious School, and from 1655 Christoph Wittich taught theology there, the ablest of the Dutch divines who held that the philosophy of Descartes could be joined to Reformed theology, and that where Scripture speaks of the natural world, as of the sun standing still, it accommodates itself to the common speech of men rather than teaching natural philosophy. The Voetian party answered that this makes a philosophy the judge of what Scripture may be allowed to mean. The dictionary sides with them. A rule of interpretation taken from outside the text and allowed to decide in advance which statements of Scripture are real assertions has conceded the authority it claims to defend, and the Nijmegen school is where that was argued out in the quietest and therefore most persuasive form.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines accommodation as adjustment or adaptation; philosophy as the knowledge of natural causes; to assert as to affirm positively; and interpretation as the act of explaining.
webster_full: ACCOMMODATION, n. Fitness; adaptation; adjustment of differences; the act of fitting one thing to another.
PHILOSOPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of the phenomena or effects of nature, and of their causes.
ASSERT, v. To affirm positively; to declare with assurance; to maintain or defend by words or measures.
INTERPRETATION, n. The act of interpreting; explanation of what is obscure; the sense given by an interpreter.
ACADEMY, n. A school or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: Chief town of Gelderland, retaken for the republic in 1591, whose Illustrious School under Christoph Wittich from 1655 became a seat of Cartesian theology.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is Cartesian accommodation, and the dictionary names it as a corruption of the doctrine of Scripture rather than as a harmless opinion about astronomy. Wittich and his party granted the new philosophy the right to decide which of Scripture's statements are assertions and which are condescensions to vulgar speech; once that right is granted the principle has no boundary, and later ages applied it to the creation, the flood and the resurrection. The apostolic warning is exactly to the point: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture is inspired in all that it affirms, and that the test of any interpretation is the text itself and not the system brought to it. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) admits no class of statements exempted in advance, and the men who wrote it “spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21). The rule for trying a new philosophy is the rule for trying anything else: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20), and the judge in that court is not Descartes.

“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the Voetian answer to a philosophy made judge of the text.
